title: Trophic levels in an ecosystem biology only
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for AQA GCSE Biology (8461) (status of the source: authored-gated-unreviewed). Terms and clues: 4.7.4-c02 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.7.4-c03 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.7.4-c04 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.7.4-c05 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition. Questions: 4.7.4-q01, 4.7.4-q02, 4.7.4-q03, 4.7.4-q04, 4.7.4-q05, 4.7.4-q06, 4.7.4-q07.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

questions.stem: A food chain is: algae to mayfly larvae to minnow to pike. The pike has no predators in this ecosystem. Which statement about this food chain is correct?

options.text: The pike is a tertiary consumer.
The minnow is an apex predator.
The mayfly larvae are at level 1.
The pike is a secondary consumer.

questions.explanation: The pike is a carnivore that eats another carnivore, the minnow, so it is at trophic level 4 and is called a tertiary consumer. As it has no predators it is also an apex predator.

questions.stem: An oak tree of biomass 4000 kg supports 3000 caterpillars of total biomass 6 kg, which are eaten by 20 blue tits of total biomass 0.2 kg. Which description of the pyramid of biomass for these data is correct?

options.text: The oak tree is the widest bar, at the bottom.
The three bars are drawn with equal widths.
The oak tree is the narrowest bar, at the bottom.
The caterpillars form the bottom bar, as level 1.

questions.explanation: Trophic level 1 is at the bottom of the pyramid, and the bars represent the relative amount of biomass in each level, so the oak tree with 4000 kg forms the widest bar.

questions.stem: Approximately what percentage of the incident energy from light do producers transfer for photosynthesis?

options.text: About 10%
About 1%
About 50%
About 90%

questions.explanation: Producers are mostly plants and algae which transfer about 1% of the incident energy from light for photosynthesis.

questions.stem: A trophic level contains 6000 g of biomass. Approximately what mass of biomass is transferred to the trophic level above it?
questions.explanation: Only approximately 10% of the biomass from each trophic level is transferred to the level above it, and 10% of 6000 g is 600 g.

questions.stem: Which statement explains why biomass is lost between one trophic level and the next?

options.text: The uneaten parts of the prey are the main loss.
Glucose used in respiration is passed on.
Much of the glucose is used in respiration.
Producers use 10% of the light energy.

questions.explanation: Large amounts of glucose are used in respiration, and the carbon dioxide and water produced are lost as waste, so this material is not transferred to the trophic level above.

questions.stem: A trophic level contains 800 g of biomass. The trophic level above it contains 40 g of biomass. What is the efficiency of the biomass transfer between these two levels?
questions.explanation: The efficiency is the biomass transferred as a percentage of the mass available: 40 divided by 800, multiplied by 100, gives 5%.

questions.stem: A food chain is: grass to rabbits to foxes. Which statement about this food chain is correct?

options.text: Similar numbers of rabbits and foxes live here.
Far fewer foxes than rabbits are supported.
More foxes than rabbits live here, as foxes hunt.
Nearly all the rabbits' biomass reaches foxes.

questions.explanation: Only approximately 10% of the biomass from each trophic level is transferred to the level above it, so much less biomass is available to the foxes and fewer organisms can be supported at that level.
